topic.subject: general
topic.title: Mobile phones and radiation myths
topic.scope: how phones use radio waves, non-ionising vs ionising radiation, screen time and eyes, battery safety, common myths

nodes.name: How phones communicate using radio waves
Phones send signals as radio waves
Radio waves travel at speed of light
Phone power rises when signal is weak
Radio waves are low-energy, non-ionising
external_prereqs: energy of waves depends on frequency

nodes.name: X-rays and gamma rays are ionising
Phone radio waves cannot break DNA bonds
Phones do not make food or body radioactive

misconceptions.statement: Phones send voice through wires hidden in the air or the ground.
misconceptions.why: Old landline telephones used wires, so students assume all calls need a wired path.
misconceptions.fix: A phone changes your voice into a signal and sends it as radio waves through air to a tower. Wires are used only after the tower.

probe.question: How does your voice leave the phone and reach the tower?
probe.wrong_answer: Through thin wires under the ground from the phone.

misconceptions.root_belief: old technology rules apply to new technology

misconceptions.statement: Radio waves are sound waves, so they need air to travel.
misconceptions.why: Both are called waves and both carry voice and music.
misconceptions.fix: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves and can travel through vacuum, while sound needs a medium. Radio waves carry the voice as a signal.

probe.question: Can phone signals travel in empty space?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they are sound waves and need air.

misconceptions.root_belief: things that do similar jobs are the same kind
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students confusing sound and light or electromagnetic waves

misconceptions.statement: Radio waves from phones travel slowly, like sound.
misconceptions.why: Students link voice with sound, which they know travels slowly.
misconceptions.fix: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 3 lakh km per second, far faster than sound.

probe.question: Which is faster, a phone signal or sound in air?
probe.wrong_answer: Sound, because the voice is sound.

misconceptions.root_belief: the carried thing and its carrier behave alike

misconceptions.statement: The phone connects to a satellite for every normal call.
misconceptions.why: Satellites are often shown in news and ads about mobile networks.
misconceptions.fix: Ordinary calls go from the phone to the nearest mobile tower, then through the network. Satellites are used only in special cases such as satellite phones.

probe.question: Where does your phone send its signal first in a normal call?
probe.wrong_answer: To a satellite in space.

misconceptions.root_belief: the most advanced thing must be doing the job

misconceptions.statement: A phone sends out the same power at all times, even in a good signal area.
misconceptions.why: Students do not see that phones adjust their power.
misconceptions.fix: A phone uses more power when the signal is weak and less when it is strong. This is why the battery drains faster in poor coverage.

probe.question: Why does the battery drain faster in a lift or basement?
probe.wrong_answer: It does not; the phone always sends the same power.

misconceptions.root_belief: devices work at one fixed setting

misconceptions.statement: All radiation, including phone radio waves, is dangerous like nuclear radiation.
misconceptions.why: The word radiation in news is linked to nuclear accidents and bombs.
misconceptions.fix: Radiation has many kinds. Radio waves, light and microwaves have low energy and cannot ionise atoms, unlike X-rays and gamma rays.

probe.question: Is the radiation from a phone as harmful as radiation from a nuclear plant?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all radiation is equally harmful.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas about radiation and radioactivity

misconceptions.statement: A stronger or more powerful phone signal always has higher energy per wave like X-rays.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up loudness or strength of a signal with the energy of each wave.
misconceptions.fix: Energy of each wave depends on frequency, not on how strong the signal is. Radio waves stay low-energy even when the signal is strong.

probe.question: Can a very strong radio signal turn into X-rays?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if the signal is strong enough it becomes X-rays.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Only nuclear bombs and power plants produce ionising radiation.
misconceptions.why: News stories link ionising radiation only to nuclear events.
misconceptions.fix: X-rays in hospitals, radioactive rocks, and the Sun's ultraviolet rays also ionise. Doses from medical X-rays are small and controlled.

probe.question: Name a place where you could meet ionising radiation.
probe.wrong_answer: Only a nuclear power plant or bomb.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rare thing is found only in dramatic places

misconceptions.statement: Non-ionising radiation means no radiation, so it has no effect at all.
misconceptions.why: The prefix non suggests absence.
misconceptions.fix: Non-ionising radiation is real energy; it can warm things, as in a microwave oven. It just cannot knock electrons out of atoms.

probe.question: Does non-ionising radiation carry any energy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, non-ionising means there is no radiation.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Phone radiation slowly damages DNA and causes cancer in people who talk a lot.
misconceptions.why: Social media and forwarded messages repeat this fear without evidence.
misconceptions.fix: Radio waves do not have enough energy to break DNA. WHO says no confirmed health harm from phone use has been found, though research continues.

probe.question: Can long phone calls break DNA in the body?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the radiation breaks DNA and causes cancer.

misconceptions.root_belief: scary claims repeated often must be true

misconceptions.statement: Living near a mobile tower makes people sick because of its strong radiation.
misconceptions.why: Tower fear spreads in neighbourhoods and the tower looks big and powerful.
misconceptions.fix: Signal from a tower is very weak by the time it reaches homes and is well below safety limits set in India. It is non-ionising and cannot damage cells.

probe.question: Does a tower on the roof across the road cause illness?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, big towers give out a lot of radiation that harms people.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Keeping a phone under the pillow at night will certainly give you brain damage.
misconceptions.why: Warnings forwarded online link phones near the head with harm.
misconceptions.fix: Phone radio waves cannot damage brain cells. A phone near the bed may disturb sleep through notifications and light, which is the real concern.

probe.question: What is the main risk of sleeping with a phone under your pillow?
probe.wrong_answer: Radiation will damage the brain.

misconceptions.root_belief: closeness to a source means certain harm

misconceptions.statement: Phones make food or water radioactive if kept near them.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up radio waves with radioactivity because the words sound alike.
misconceptions.fix: Radio waves cannot make anything radioactive. Radioactivity comes from unstable atomic nuclei.

probe.question: If you keep a bottle next to a phone, does the water become radioactive?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the radiation makes it radioactive.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding words mean related things
misconceptions.source_hint: research on confusion between irradiation and contamination

misconceptions.statement: A person who has been near a phone is carrying radiation in their body afterwards.
misconceptions.why: Students think that exposure leaves radiation stored in the body.
misconceptions.fix: Radio waves pass or get absorbed as tiny heat and do not stay stored. The body is not radioactive after exposure.

probe.question: Is a person radioactive after a long phone call?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the radiation stays inside the body.

misconceptions.root_belief: exposure to a source leaves it inside you
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students mixing up irradiation and contamination

misconceptions.statement: A phone that feels warm is giving out dangerous radiation.
misconceptions.why: Warmth is felt, so students link it with the invisible radiation.
misconceptions.fix: Warmth mostly comes from the battery, chips and screen working. It is not a sign of harmful radiation.

probe.question: Your phone is warm while gaming. What is the main reason?
probe.wrong_answer: It is giving out harmful radiation.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Looking at a screen for hours can make you permanently blind.
misconceptions.why: Adults warn strongly about screens and this exaggerates the harm.
misconceptions.fix: Long screen use can tire the eyes and cause dryness, but it does not cause blindness in normal use. Rest and breaks help.

probe.question: Can too much mobile use make you blind for life?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, screens burn the eye and cause blindness.

misconceptions.root_belief: too much of anything causes permanent damage

misconceptions.statement: Wearing spectacles for long makes eyes weaker and dependent on them.
misconceptions.why: Students notice power rises over years and blame the glasses.
misconceptions.fix: Spectacles do not weaken the eyes. They only correct vision, and power can change as the eye grows.

probe.question: Do glasses make eyes weaker?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the eyes become lazy and weak.

misconceptions.root_belief: correlated events mean one causes the other

misconceptions.statement: Eyes feel tired from screens because the screen emits harmful rays into them.
misconceptions.why: Students look for a hidden radiation cause for any discomfort.
misconceptions.fix: Tired eyes come mostly from staring without blinking, close focus and glare, not from harmful rays.

probe.question: Why do eyes get dry after hours of gaming?
probe.wrong_answer: Harmful rays from the screen dry them.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see must be the cause

misconceptions.statement: Short-sightedness is caused only by reading in dim light or using screens.
misconceptions.why: Parents commonly blame light and screens for poor eyesight.
misconceptions.fix: Myopia is linked to genes, too much close work and too little outdoor time. Playing outside in daylight helps protect children's eyes.

probe.question: What is the only cause of short-sightedness in children?
probe.wrong_answer: Reading in dim light and using screens.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: public health studies on myopia and outdoor time

misconceptions.statement: One long break after many hours of screen time is as good as short breaks every so often.
misconceptions.why: Students think total rest time matters, not how often.
misconceptions.fix: Short breaks often, like looking far away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes, relax the eye muscles better.

probe.question: Which is better for tired eyes: a 20-second break every 20 minutes or one hour break after six hours?
probe.wrong_answer: The one long break, because the rest time is the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the total amount matters, not spacing

misconceptions.statement: Charging a phone overnight makes it explode, so it must be unplugged at exactly 100%.
misconceptions.why: Viral videos of burning phones are linked to charging.
misconceptions.fix: Modern phones stop charging when full. Fires come mostly from faulty chargers or damaged batteries, not from normal overnight charging.

probe.question: Will a phone with a good charger explode if left charging overnight?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will overcharge and explode.

misconceptions.root_belief: a dramatic event shows what normally happens

misconceptions.statement: Any cheap charger that fits the port is as safe as the original charger.
misconceptions.why: Students think if the plug fits, the electrical specs must match.
misconceptions.fix: Poor chargers may give wrong voltage or lack safety checks and can overheat the battery. Use a certified charger.

probe.question: Is a loose roadside charger as safe as the company charger?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if it fits, it is the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: looking the same means working the same

misconceptions.statement: A puffed-up phone battery is fine to keep using if the phone still works.
misconceptions.why: Students judge safety only by whether the phone works.
misconceptions.fix: A swollen battery has gas inside from faulty chemical reactions and can catch fire. Stop using it and get it replaced.

probe.question: Your phone back is bulging but works fine. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Keep using it since it works.

misconceptions.root_belief: if it works, it is safe

misconceptions.statement: A phone gets hot only when it is being charged.
misconceptions.why: Students notice warmth most while charging.
misconceptions.fix: The phone also warms during gaming, video, and in hot sun, as the chips and battery use current.

probe.question: When can a phone get warm?
probe.wrong_answer: Only while it is charging.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
